lessons.title: Communication & Tech Evolution
lessons.summary: Learn the three core elements of a communication system and trace communication from ancient beacons to 5G/6G and IoE.

slideBullets.text: From the very origins and subsequent development of human society, communication has remained a constant companion. Since the 1970s and 1980s, human society has entered the information age. For those of us living in this era, the necessity of communication is beyond question.
In this course, communication refers to the transmission of information through a data communication network.

This course introduces the concepts of communication and data communication networks, network types and typical topologies, network devices and their functions, and the process of information transmission. It also provides a brief introduction to network engineering and the role of network engineers.
Upon completion of this course, you will be able to:
Understand the concepts related to network communication and data communication networks.
Understand different types of networks and topologies.
Differentiate network devices of different types and understand their basic functions.
Describe the information transfer process.
Understand the concepts related to network engineering and network engineers.

diagram.altText: The essence of communication lies in the transmission and exchange of information between two or ⚫ more points—that is, the conveyance and interaction of information among people, between people and objects, and among objects, facilitated through certain media and actions. notes.text: In addition to the communication system, communication has the following key elements:
Information: content to be transmitted, which can be in any form, such as voice, text, graphics, and data.
Communication protocol: rules (such as language, encoding mode, and communication standard) agreed by both parties to ensure that information can be correctly encoded, transmitted, and decoded.

notes.text: Ancient times: In this era, communication relied entirely on the most basic natural media, human power, and animal power.

Visual and auditory communication: such as beacon towers, smoke signals, drum beats, and horns. These methods conveyed extremely limited information (usually prearranged signals), covered short distances, and were easily affected by weather and terrain.

Postal communication: Post stations and postal systems were established, and letters were transported by people and horses. This allowed for the transmission of larger amounts of information, but the speed was extremely slow, often taking days or even months.

Electrical era: From the mid-19th century to the early 20th century, the invention and application of electricity completely transformed communication, allowing information to travel at the speed of light for the first time.
Telegraph (1830s–1840s): For the first time, people were able to communicate instantaneously over long distances (across continents or oceans). Information was transmitted through electrical wires.
Telephone (1870s): Real-time, two-way voice communication was realized, making communication more natural and direct.

Radio (1890s): Radio freed communication from the constraints of physical lines, laying the foundation for mobile communication and broadcasting. The subsequent development of AM/FM radio and television became the dominant mass media of the 20th century.

Information era: From the mid-20th century to the present, the invention of transistors, integrated circuits, and computer technologies has propelled communication into a new era of digitalization and networking.

Computers and the Internet (1960s–1990s): The birth of the Advanced Research Projects Agency Network (ARPANET) and the adoption of Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol (TCP/IP) marked the beginning of the Internet era. Communication expanded beyond human-to-human, evolving into machine-to-machine and network-to-network interactions.
Mobile communication (1980s–present):
1st generation (1G): analog voice communication, enabling people to make calls while moving.
2nd generation (2G): digital voice communication, introducing Short Message Service (SMS).
3rd generation (3G): mobile Internet access, enabling users to browse web pages and send and receive emails.
4th generation (4G): the true era of mobile broadband, with explosive growth in applications such as smooth HD video, online gaming, and mobile payment.

5th generation (5G): ultra-high speed, ultra-low latency, and massive connectivity. Beyond human communication, it aims to empower vertical industries such as the Internet of Things (IoT), autonomous driving, telemedicine, and industrial automation.
1G/2G/3G/4G/5G: 1st/2nd/3rd/4th/5th-Generation Mobile Communication Technology
The era of Internet of Everything (IoE): Communication technologies continue to accelerate in development.

Deepening of 5G and exploration of 6G: Enhanced versions such as 5G-A/5.5G will further improve performance. 6G is expected to be commercially deployed around 2030, aiming to support holographic communication, sensory interconnection, and digital twins, realizing "intelligent connectivity of everything."

Integration of IoT and Artificial Intelligence (AI): Communication will expand from humans to all things in the world. AI will empower communication networks with intelligent resource scheduling, fault prediction, and security protection, making networks more efficient and reliable.

challenge.prompt: Arrange these communication milestones in chronological order from oldest to newest (Slide 6):
items: Visual and auditory signals (Beacon fires, ~3000 BCE)
challenge.explanation: Communication progressed from Ancient times (~3000 BCE beacons) -> Electrical era (1830s telegraph) -> Information era (1960s–1970s ARPANET) -> IoE era (late 2010s 5G and beyond).

slideBullets.text: A network topology is a structured layout of how various network devices (such as computers, routers,

diagram.altText: and switches) are connected through transmission media (such as twisted pairs and optical fibers). A network topology diagram describes the physical or logical structure of a network, which is essential in network engineering. ... ...

diagram.altText: Networks can be classified into bus, star, ring, tree, full-mesh, and partial-mesh networks based on the ⚫ network topology. In real-world networks, different topologies are often combined to strike a trade-off among cost, ⚫ performance, and reliability needs. Bus network Star network Ring network Combined network Tree network Full-mesh network Partial-mesh network

notes.text: Bus network: All nodes are connected through a bus (such as a coaxial cable).
Advantage: Installation is easy with minimal cables required. Generally, a fault on a node does not affect the communication of the entire network.
Disadvantage: The failure of the bus affects the communication of the entire network. Information sent by a node can be received by all other nodes, which is insecure.
Star network: All nodes are connected through a central node.
Advantage: New nodes can be easily added to the network. Communication data must be forwarded through the central node, facilitating network monitoring.
Disadvantage: The failure of the central node affects the communication of the entire network.
Ring network: All nodes are connected to form a closed ring.
Advantage: Fewer cables are required.
Disadvantage: Adding a new node is inconvenient. You need to break the original ring before inserting the new node to form a new ring.
Tree network: actually a hierarchical star topology.
Advantage: Multiple star networks can be quickly connected, facilitating network expansion.
Disadvantage: The higher the node, the more severe network issues caused by the node's failure.
Full-mesh network: All nodes are interconnected through cables.
Advantage: It features high reliability and communication efficiency.
Disadvantage: Each node requires a large number of physical ports and cables for network connections. It is costly and difficult to scale.
Partial-mesh network: Only key nodes are interconnected.
Advantage: The cost is lower than that of a full-mesh topology.
Disadvantage: The reliability is lower than that of a full-mesh topology.

challenge.prompt: Match each network topology to its defining Huawei textbook characteristic (Slide 10):

pairs.right: Failure of the shared bus affects the entire network; insecure
Easy to add nodes & monitor, but central node is a single point of failure
Uses fewer cables, but adding a node requires breaking the ring
Highest reliability & efficiency, but costly and hard to scale

challenge.explanation: Real-world networks combine topologies to balance cost, performance, and reliability. Star is easy to expand; Full-mesh maximizes redundancy at high port/cable cost.

notes.text: The figure shows a typical enterprise office campus network.

In the campus equipment room, egress devices such as routers and firewalls are deployed to enable secure communication with external networks. At the same time, core campus devices such as core switches and WACs are also placed there to implement internal data interconnection across the entire campus network.

Midsize and large enterprises often have independent data centers. Data center devices such as switches and servers are usually located in an independent data center equipment room and physically connected to the campus core, providing various application services and data storage for internal or external users.

On each office floor, an access switch can be installed to connect APs or wired terminals within that floor's office area for office network access. The APs then provide wireless signals to allow wireless terminals in the office area to access the network.

Based on their functions, modular devices support Main Processing Units (MPUs), Switch Fabric Units (SFUs), and ⚫ Line Processing Units (LPUs). diagram.altText: The process of virtual information transfer shares many similarities with the transfer of real physical ⚫ objects. Item Parcel Parcel pickup Parcel sorting Parcel sorting Parcel pickup Parcel Item station center center station Transportation Packet Packet Data Data Data Data Computer Computer Gateway Router Internet Router Gateway Computer Computer

notes.text: Packing and labeling (sender):
Sender: The item is packaged into a parcel, and a shipping label containing the sender's and recipient's addresses is attached.

Data sender: The application encapsulates the original "data payload" by adding a "header" and a "trailer" to form a packet. The key information in the packet is the sender's and receiver's addresses, that is, the "source address" and the "destination address."
Local dispatch (first transfer station):

Parcel pickup station: The parcel is received by a courier and placed in the local parcel pickup station. The station determines where to send the parcel based on the recipient's address and notifies the next courier to collect it.

Gateway: The packet travels through the network cable to the "gateway." The gateway decapsulates the packet, reads the destination address, and then re-encapsulates it. Depending on the destination address, the packet leaves the local network and is sent to different "routers."
Network sorting and transmission (intermediate node):

Parcel sorting center and transportation: The city's parcel sorting center forwards parcels to the destination city's sorting center using different transportation methods, based on the recipient's address.

Routers and the Internet backbone: The intermediate routers continuously decapsulate and encapsulate the packet, and then send the packet to the Internet backbone for transmission. Finally, the packet is sent to the destination network.
Final delivery and reception (receiver)

Recipient: The sorting center in the destination city checks the recipient's address, dispatches the parcel to the appropriate parcel pickup station, and finally the courier delivers it to the recipient. The recipient opens the parcel, confirms the item is intact, and accepts it. The entire delivery process is complete.

Data receiver: The packet arrives at the gateway of the destination computer's network, where it is decapsulated and encapsulated again, then forwarded to the appropriate computer based on the destination address. The computer verifies the packet, and if correct, accepts it and passes the data payload to the corresponding application for processing. A complete network communication process is thus finished.

diagram.altText: Term Description Data payload Actual information intended to be transmitted Packet Data unit exchanged and transmitted on a network. Header Segment of information added before the data payload. Trailer Segment of information added after the data payload. Process of adding a header and a trailer to a data payload to form a new Encapsulation packet. Process of removing the header and trailer from a packet to obtain the Decapsulation data payload. Gateway A device that connects two different networks. End device of a data communication system, serving as a sender or Terminal receiver of data.

notes.text: Data payload: It can be understood as the actual information intended to be transmitted. In fact, within a layered communication structure, the data unit (packet) passed from an upper-layer protocol to a lower-layer protocol can be regarded as the data payload of the lower-layer protocol.

Packet: The unit of data exchanged and transmitted on a network, with a certain internal format. It usually has the basic structure of "header + data payload + trailer." During transmission, the format and content of the packet may change.
Header: To enable better information delivery, when assembling a packet, the segment of information added before the data payload is collectively referred to as the header.

Trailer: To enable better information delivery, when assembling a packet, the segment of information added after the data payload is collectively referred to as the trailer. Note that many packets do not have a trailer.

Encapsulation: A technique used in layered protocols. When a lower-layer protocol receives a message from an upper-layer protocol, it attaches that message to the data payload portion of the lower-layer message.
Decapsulation: The reverse process of encapsulation, which is to remove the header and trailer of a packet to obtain the data payload.

Gateway: A network device used to enable communication between networks that adopt different architectures or protocols. It provides functions such as protocol conversion, routing selection, and data exchange. A gateway is a term named according to its deployment location and function, rather than a specific device type.

Terminal: An end device in a data communication system, acting as either the sender or receiver of data. It provides the necessary functions for user access and protocol operations, and can be a computer, server, mobile phone, or the like.

challenge.prompt: Which TWO statements accurately describe data encapsulation and common terms? (Slides 28–29)
options: Encapsulation adds a header (and optionally a trailer) to a data payload
A gateway is a specific physical hardware box model with no routing function
Decapsulation removes the header and trailer to recover the data payload

challenge.explanation: Encapsulation wraps a payload with a header/trailer, and decapsulation strips them off. Note that Huawei explicitly points out many packets do not have a trailer, and 'gateway' is named by its deployment location/function rather than a single device type.

slideBullets.text: This course describes the concepts of network communication and data communication networks. The basic function of data communication networks is to implement network communication.

To understand data communication networks, it is necessary to grasp their fundamental concepts and key components, including network topologies, network types, and the various network devices and their functions.

Finally, this course also introduces network engineering and network engineers. In addition to fundamental professional qualities, a network engineer also needs to acquire relevant skills and knowledge. Huawei datacom certification provides a specialized learning path to achieve this.
